irregularity, if you like-
By our officer.
By our officer?
An officer of parliament.

The officer of my right
hon. friend as well as of myself.

But appointed by the
government.

I am glad to hear him say that only for that reason this petition must be received. But if all other officers made mistakes, would all the petitions have to be received here? If, for instance, a political party desired to exercise partisanship to the highest degree in a house where the government majority would be forty or fifty over the party on the other side, and if all petitions came to the House instead of being heard by the legally constituted tribunals of the land, would it not be possible for a partisan majority to oblige almost all of the members in the minority to vacate their seats? That certainly would happen. It sometimes did happen many years ago, and that is why parliament in its wisdom de-
Peace River Election

cided that these questions should not be dealt with here, but should be decided by judicial and independent tribunals. If those legally constituted courts find any irregularity or any criminal act on the part of any officer, it is the duty of the judge hearing the matter to report to Mr. Speaker, who reads the report to the House at the opening of the next session. Then is the time for parliament to judge the act of that officer. The petition before you, Sir, is worded in plain English. It is a request that the hon. member for Peace River leave his seat and give it to his defeated opponent in his last election. Before he is asked to do that, we should not look at what took place in one particular polling subdivision, but the court legally empowered to do so should consider what took place in every polling subdivision, and when that has been determined it will be time for parliament to decide wbat punishment should be meted out to any guilty officer and consider any amendment that should be made to the election act. There is one amendment which never should be made. That is an amendment which would take out of the hands of an impartial judge or tribunal and refer to party politicians all matters connected with the election of members to this House.

May I be permitted to say a word
on the point of order? I will endeavour to discuss the point raised by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) without wandering as far afield as the hon. Minister of Customs and Excise (Mr. Boivin) has done in the remarks he has addressed to the House.
The question in a way is a simple but very interesting one. It is at the same time a most important question and involves the right of a British subject to petition this parliament, a right whioh is laid down by all constitutional writers as an inherent right in our citizenship. A British subject has lodged a petition before this parliament, and the question is whether or not his petition should be received. That, I understand, Mr. Speaker, is the sole question raised this afternoon by the Prime Minister. I am not going to discuss the merits of the case as presented by my hon. friend from West Calgary (Mr. Bennett), but will content myself briefly and solely with a discussion of the right of Mr. Collins to lay a petition on the table of this House and have it received by the House. If our constitutional rights are to be brushed aside with the indifference which has been displayed this afternoon by hon. members opposite, I think the time has come when 
we should lay down some definite rule upon the matter. That the right exists there can be no question. A citizen of this country desires to exercise that right; the question is should parliament refuse him that right.
The Prime Minister has cited certain precedents to the House. In the two earlier precedents, that of 1874 and of 1881, it would appear that the Speakers of those days ruled that the petition should not be received. These were early cases, but I point out, Mr. Speaker, that the earlier decisions have been superseded by what took place in this House in connection with the Queen's election case, I think, in 1887 or 1888, followed by another decision, in the year 1900 known as the West Huron election case. I am leaving out for the moment the Coderre case, because I understand that no petition was presented in that case. I take my information on that point from the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald). Let us turn to the two more recent cases in which petitions were presented and received, notably the Queen's case in 1887 and the West Huron case in 1900. If in the earlier cases the petitions were not received by the House should we be bound by them in the face of what was done in the two more recent cases? Surely the earlier cases have been overruled and superseded, and the law and custom of this parliament at this moment has been settled by the course adopted in both the Queen's and Huron cases, where the petitions were received by this House.
I do not say anything as to the ultimate fate of the petition. I say nothing whatever as to what may or may not be done, or what may be the fate of any motion which may be made hereafter in respect of this petition. But what is our duty at the present moment? I can only repeat what has been said by the hon. member for West Calgary in support of the precedents Which have been cited. These precedents were supported by parliament. Objection was taken in the Queen's election case that the petition should not be received. The Minister of Justice of that day was inclined to think there was great force in the argument, but he informed the House that, having regard to the whole situation, he believed the petition should be received. It was received and was referred to tlhe committee on Privileges and Elections. Is there any reason, Mr. Speaker, for departing from that decision in the present instance?
Then in the West Huron case in 1900 the petition was likewise received by the House. Subsequently it was thrown out or turned down, but it had been received by the House.

Peace River Election
Is there a reason for departing from the established practice of the House on these two occasions? These are the two most recent cases. This petition does deal both directly and indirectly with an officer of this House; there can be no question of that. I am not referring to the prayer of the petition, in which the petitioner claims the seat, but I am referring to the allegations which are made on the face of the petition, the statements of fact that appear upon it. Nothing is more clear than the fact that the conduct of an officer of this House is very gravely brought into question, and I do not think anyone would argue for a moment that this House has not the sole supervision and control of its own officers. That gives us jurisdiction and the right to receive the petition, on the ground, if on no other, that the conduct of one of the officers of this House is impugned. Rule 80 is a very definite rule on that point and reads:
If it shall appear that any person hath Ibeen elected and returned a member of this House, or endeavoured so to be, by bribery, or any other corrupt practices, this House will proceed with the utmost seventy against all such persons as shall have been wilfully concerned in such bribery or other corrupt practices.
What is the first clause of the rule? It provides that if it shall appear that any person has been connected with bribery or other corrupt practice this House <hall speedily inquire into the matter. We have the right to inquire in regard to our own officers; we have the right to discipline, to punish our own officers. Notwithstanding that the courts of the land have punished an officer of this House for a criminal offence, we still have the right to summon him to the bar of the House or before the committee and to deal with him as we see fit. Rule 80 is in our rule book expressly to deal with a case such as that which is now before Your Honour.
I submit that on the point of order there is little to be urged in support of it and much that can be urged against it. I am not going to attempt any discussion of the merits or demerits of the question in connection with the election contest in Peace River. I know nothing of the facts save what I have read in the newspapers or heard from the language of the petition. The petitioner has made it appear, in the spirit of rule 80, that a certain condition existed during that contest rendering it the duty of this parliament to make an inquiry. I submit that on the question of order Your Honour should have no hesitation in deciding that the last two precedents, the cases of Queen's and Huron, are now the established practice of this House and should be followed in tms instance.
If the petition is received the next step is of course a motion. I do not know what might be said on the motion, whether it should be referred to a committee or not. The argument will no doubt take place upon that motion; but surely we are not going to deny a British subject the right which is inherent in his citizenship, namely, that of lodging a petition before this parliament and of having that petition received. That is all we ask.

Mt. Speaker, as the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) has just said, the question which is now before the House is not that of the merits or demerits of the respective contesting parties before the courts in the Peace River constituency, but simply the point of deciding whether the petition presented by the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) should or should not be received.
This afternoon, as in all matters of this nature, we have had abundant evidence of the wisdom of those who in 1874 decided that election matters should be taken away from the competency of parliament. We have listened to veiy learned lawyers on both sides and not to my surprise I have noticed that instinctively political feeling has crept into the arguments which we have heard. What conclusion must we draw, what inference must we arrive at, other than that if Your Honour comes to the conclusion that the petition has anything to do with the election itself, Your Honour should follow the rule laid down by your predecessors and decide that the petition should not be allowed to be received by the House?
Any lawyer conversant with parliamentary law or constitutional precedent must reach the conclusion, first, that parliament decided years ago-and that decision has been confirmed and ratified under many circumstances -not to interfere any longer in matters merely electoral. And why so? Because when parliament decided controverted elections, either when the House was sitting as a whole or when the House delegated its powers to a select committee, parliament ceased to exercise purely legislative powers or functions and exercised judicial powers. There is one great underlying principle of the British constitution, and its greatest safeguard-this the hon. member for West Calgary will not deny -namely, that executive, legislative and judicial powers should not interfere with one another. I say with pride that the judiciary of Canada can be compared favourably with the judiciary of any other country. Why should we, especially in view of the most
Peace River Election

peculiar and special conditions under which this parliament has met, take away from judges, take away from duly constituted and established courts, a question which belongs to a judicial tribunal, a court presided over by a judge, merely for the purpose of having witnesses bring before a committee, evidence which in all probability cannot be judged by the members of that committee without their being biased by political feeling? There is no doubt that parliament has divested itself of the function of judging cases of controverted elections. The only reason for the receiving of this petition would be that advanced by the hon. member for West Calgary, namely, that it deals not with the election itself but with the conduct or behaviour of an officer of this House. If my hon. friend is right in that contention the petition should be received. If Your Honour comes to the conclusion that his contention is not right, the petition should not be received.
What is the petition? The hon. member for West Calgary has read it; he has read not only the allegations which are the basis for the conclusion, but the conclusion itself of the petitioner Collins. The petition, therefore, is divided into two parts which must not be confused. The first part consists of allegations of fraud committed by certain electoral officers. There is no doubt that parliament has absolute authority to deal with those officers. We can deal with them either directly by calling them before a committee or before the House, or indirectly under the provisions of the Elections Act or the Controverted Elections Act, when a report is sent in to Your Honour giving Your Honour the facts and knowledge of any fraud committed by those officers. But that petition does not ask thait any officer in that constituency who might have committed fraud be punished by this House or by the committee. The conclusion of the petition is the essential section, and an examination of it will lead Your Honour to a decision on this point of order. The conclusion is, not that Robb or any other officer should be punished or reprimanded, but that the sitting member be removed and that the petitioner himself be given his seat. The conclusion is, therefore, that we as a House of Commons, either ourselves or through a committee, shall supersede the judicial tribunals of the country in deciding who shall be the member to represent in parliament the constituency of Peace River. I do not think that a single hon. member in this House this afternoon, no matter on which side he sits, will deny that the petition presented by the hon. member for West Calgary, if accepted, would have 
that effect. We are to decide who shall represent Peace River in the House of Commons, according to the petition. Well, in 1874 parliament decided once for all that these matters should no longer be within its competency.
I come now to the last point. Hon. gentlemen opposite ask, why should we not receive the petition? Well, Mr. Speaker, the receipt of the petition would be followed by a motion for its reference to the committee. There is another principle of parliamentary law which cannot be contradicted by any lawyer in this House, and that principle is that the House, under the direction of its Speaker, shall take no action and follow no line of procedure without having a practical object in view. We are not here to waste time. We are not here to lose or waste the money of the Canadian people who sent us to parliament. Every resolution thait comes before the House, every petition that is presented for the consideration of parliament, must have a definite object in view. That principle is well established. But what would be the practical object of this petition even if it were received?
Justice.

My hon. friend from Ottawa says, justice. I am also of his opinion, and I will show before I get through how justice coincides with my contention. What, I ask, would be the practical outcome of the acceptance of this petition? The hon. member for West Calgary would move that it be referred to the committee on Privileges and Elections and the House would decide one way or the other. If ithe House decided to refer it to the committee, the committee, unless we ignored all precedents that have been established during the past fifty years, could not possibly decide who (the sitting member should be, because that is a matter for the courts.
In conclusion let me say that this is not a matter of politics; it is a matter purely of law. In the first place I say that the petition should not be received, for its conclusion is a request that this House decide a controverted election; and, secondly, I am opposed to its reception for the reason that even if it were referred to the committee the committee could not take any practical action upon it. Now, as to the justice of the matter. Here we have a fellow member who enjoys the esteem of every hon. gentleman in this House, and as opposed to him there is the petitioner, against whom I have nothing to say but who claims the seat. I understand that there was also a third candidate. Are we then, if we

Peace River Election
have any feeling of justice and fair play, to constitute ourselves a tribunal, setting aside all precedents governing cases of this kind, and decide this matter in the interests of one party or another? The hon. member for West Calgary observed, indeed, that it was important that Collins should be here, because if he were the government might be out. I do not care whether the government remains in power or goes out, but I stand for the principles of fairness and justice, principles which were written into our statute books in 1874 and which have been observed ever since. What was good enough for Sir John A. Macdonald and Sir John Thompson, what was good enough for Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Sir Robert Borden, is good enough for the smaller men who sit now in the House in their stead.

I have sat this afternoon nearly three hours listening to this debate, which has been largely between lawyers; for apart from the speech of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) no one so far has spoken who was not of the legal profession. As an ordinary member of the House who has had no legal training, but who trusts that he has an appreciable sense of fair play, I wish to add a few words to what has been said.
The Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon) in his concluding remarks declared that this was entirely a matter of law. I do not share that view, Mr. Speaker. I contend that it is absolutely a question affecting the honour of parliament and the rights of the people of Canada, in relation to the composition of this House. The action of the Prime Minister in raising the point of order as to whether or not the petition should be received may be briefly summed up. The motion, shorn of all its ornamentation, will in effect allow the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy) to retain his seat in the House of Commons.

speechtext: I am discussing a point of order. I hardly see the necessity for the heated remarks of the Prime Minister. Let me say at once that I did not intend to cast any reflection whatever upon him, though I see he did not hesitate to reflect upon myself. I did not seek to imply at all that: there was any base motive underlying his: procedure this afternoon. The point I am trying to make is that the logical conclusion of his motion will be to enable the hon. member for Peace River to retain the seat which he now holds and to which, as some of us contend, he is not entitled. That is the sum and substance of what I was saying. I did not intend at all to reflect in any way upon the Prime Minister. As a matter of fact, if I cared to do so, I might point out many instances in which he has reflected on me. I have no hesitation in meeting the Prime Minister here or elsewhere. However, I wish to deal with this matter now from the standpoint of an ordinary member of the House, and I will not be deflected from that by the heated and unnecessary remarks of the Prime Minister.
I was pointing out tlhe actual effect of the action of the Prime Minister in trying to keep this petition from the House on a point of order. In regard to points of order I have heard the Prime Minister himself and my good friends to my left composing the Progressive party-of which the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy) is a member-many times in this House submit this argument: In the name of fair play and fair dealing we should not pay too much attention to points of order, ibut should direct ourselves to the practical issues before parliament. Practically the whole afternoon we have heard argument

as to the absolute necessity of living up to the rules of the House. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that in giving your ruling-and that is the point I am dealing with for the moment-you will be governed not only by the precedents of the past, but I have no doubt that you . will also be governed by your long parliamentary experience and your respect for the honour and high standing of this House. I believe it is not always the duty of a Speaker -if I may say so-to give a ruling which adheres strictly to precedents, especially after a debate such as this; he should also consider what is fair and just. In this case I submit there is such an opportunity for the Speaker to show his high-mindedness by not allowing himself to be controlled absolutely by precedents one way or the other.
The Minister of Customs (Mr. Boivin) pointed out that this was not a question for parliament to decide at all, but for the courts. I repeat, Sir, that to my mind this is a question for parliament to decide. It surely is one of the duties of members of this House to decide as to the character of those who ^hall sit here to legislate, and if it is their opinion that some member is illegally sitting in the House, then it seems to me it is their duty to say so. The hon. Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon) a few moments ago stated that this petition was for the purpose of unseating Mr. Kennedy and seating Mr. Collins, but that is only if the committee to which this petition would properly be referred so decided1.
The reason, Sir, why I have taken part in this debate is not because I felt I could add anything to the legal argument regarding the point of order, but because last evening after the House rose I happened to be reading a book published many years ago which dealt with a case so much like the one now before us that I thought it was worth while quoting from the volume, and I shall do so with all the greatest pleasure because my good friend' the Solicitor General has often been in the habit of citing Charles James Fox. Fox, you will remember, was a brilliant Whig, and in the election of 1784 he ran for the constituency of Middlesex. It was a two-seated constituency and there were three candidates. The bailiff, who acted as returning officer and who was a political partisan, took the attitude of refusing to make a return of the election of Fox to the House. The younger Pitt was the then prime minister of England and he supported the bailiff, contending that the bailiff was correct and need not make a return in this case. One of Fox's friends moved a motion, which I shall not read, to the effect that the bailiff must be forced to bring in the return of that election which he had so far failed' to do. Fox had

run for another seat and was a member of the House although not for the county of Middlesex. The motion was debated, and the words of Fox are So apropos to the question now before us that I propose to read them for the benefit of hon. members. Addressing the House, Fox turned to Mr. Pitt and uttered this warning:
To the right hon. gentleman over against me I will beg leave to offer a little advice.
Perhaps I might offer this advice to the Prime Minister at the present time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Hear, hear.

The Prime Minister says,
"hear, hear." He is going to take the advice after all. I sincerely hope he sees the importance of dealing with it from the national standpoint as Fox advised.
Let him 'take care that when they see all the powers of his administration employed to overwhelm an individual, men's eyes may not open sooner than they would if he conducted himself within some bounds of decent discretion, and not thus openly violate the sacred principles of the Constitution. A moderate use of his power might the longer keep people from reflecting upon the extraordinary means by which he acquired it. But if the right hon. gentleman neglects his duty, I shall not forget mine. Though he may exert all the influence of his situation to harass and persecute, he shall find that we are incapable of unbecoming submissions. There is a principle of resistance in mankind which will not brook such injuries, and a good cause and a good heart will animate men to struggle in proportion to the size of their wrongs and the grossness of (their oppressors. If the House rejects this motion and establishes .the fatal precedent that follows that rejection, I confess I shall begin to think there is little to be expected from such a House of Commons.

accept the advice of Mr. Fox?

And the advice. But I
would counsel my hon. friend not to laugh too soon, because a few days later Pitt, on the same question being brought up again, moved as an amendment that the House should adjourn, and was defeated by 162 to 124. Fox was thereupon seated for the county of Middlesex.

Now, the point I wish to make is that one hundred and forty-two years ago-in 1784- the members of the British House of Commons of that time took the high-minded stand which I particularly commend to hon. members of this House, for they voted against their leader because they felt an injustice had been done to Box, and they also felt that they should have something to say in deciding whether he should be accepted as the member for the county of. Middlesex. I believe to-day it is the duty of this House of Commons to take a similar stand, and -if I may respectfully suggest so-I believe it is the duty of the Speaker of this House to rule on the same exalted plane in this regard, so that this House of Commons shall live up to the high traditions that the British House of Commons established one hundred and forty-two years ago.

Mr. Speaker. I trust the House will excuse me for the presumption of intruding into a debate which is usually reserved only for the legal lights, but I will be very brief, and as we have wasted so much time already it will not matter if we waste a little more. I say "wasted" advisedly, because the greater part of this afternoon has been consumed, not in debating a point of order, not in hon. members addressing themselves to argument to guide you in your decision, Sir-that was done in twenty minutes; nearly all the argument was devoted to emotional appeals to this House, and possibly beyond this House to the country, but principally to the ordinary lay members, to influence them, in case your decision should be appealed from, not to decide strictly on the rights of the question at all but to regard it from a sentimental and sympathetic point of view.
If the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) will allow me to make a suggestion for his future guidance and for the benefit of those at this end of the chamber, I noticed that while speaking of the legal aspect of the question he expressed himself to hon. gentlemen opposite in a tone quite inaudible to those at any distance from him, but when he came to the sentimental appeal, we could all hear him. I would suggest that we are not so unintelligent as to not be able to understand an argument founded on law, as well as an appeal of a sentimental character.
A great deal has been said about the- I could almost use the word-iniquity of a member sitting in this House, who may possibly be found at some future time not to be entitled to his seat. I think it is generally admitted that the hon. member 14011-196
could not resign now if he wanted to; that is the law, enacted by this parliament. The procedure or law which prevents his resignation is not a mere technicality to be taken advantage of by the hon. member; it is a deliberate enactment, that a member whose seat is being contested cannot resign. The inference, I suggest, is that it was thought more important in the interests of any particular district that it should have representation in the House, even by a member afterwards found not to be entitled to the seat. At any rate that is a suggestion which appeals to me as a reason for the enactment which prevents a man from resigning while his seat is in dispute.
The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) said that this House should regul-late or have control of who should sit in it, with which statement I differ. In support of his contention he went back to 1784 for a precedent with which he asks you, Mr. Speaker, to comply, in marked contrast to his remarks of a few moments earlier when he asked you to cast precedents behind and decide in favour of the views he put forward.
The Speaker did not decide at all on that occasion; the House of Commons decided, It was not a precedent for the Speaker.

What was the purpose of
parliament in passing the Corrupt Practices Act and similar legislation? Was it not that we might be removed from any temptation to tyrannize by a political majority over the minority? It -was felt that it was unbecoming, unwise, and not calculated to be in the best interests of our institutions that we should have an opportunity of deciding who shall be a member of the House, owing to the obvious temptations of political partisanship. Therefore, as one hon. member said, we divested ourselves of the right to deal with those questions and put them entirely in the hands of the courts.
I recall a precedent; I do not go back 184 years for it, but it is within my own recollection. There was an election in British Columbia in 1898, and the House met early in 1899. They did not have party lines in those days, so I am not attacking the sincerity or integrity of any party in this House, but it was a close House, such as we have here. A couple of votes might have defeated the government, and there were two members against whose election petitions had been presented. There were some irregularities, the exact details of which I cannot at the moment recall. The House took up the ques-

Peace River Election

tion of the right of these members to occupy their seats; the question was referred to a committee and the government brought in what was called an enabling bill, declaring that these two members were legally elected, thus validating whatever irregularities had occurred. I well recall the opposition of the day, whose legal spokesman was the late Justice Eberts. I was young and innocent in those days, believing everything I heard in parliament, and I was particularly impressed with the language he used in regard to this enabling bill. The opposition fought it tooth and nail; "Nailing hon. members into their seats by the corrupt government majority" was one of the mildest epithets applied. I remember the late Justice Eberts, standing with the bill in his hand, beginning his remarks with the words, "Mr. Speaker, I hold in my hand one of the most, if not the most, corrupt pieces of legislation ever presented to this or any other legislature in the civilized world." That was the attitude taken by the opposition, and they talked for days and weeks about the impropriety and unbecoming action of the government. They said, "'W hy not leave it to the courts, where a fair and just decision would be made?" Other precedents were pointed to where men had sat in the House, although later unseated, and there was nothing to prevent that course being followed in this case. That was the attitude taken at that time, whatever its faults of logic or whatever partisanship may have been involved. I have always since been convinced that it is highly desirable that no political party should be enabled to exercise control which would certainly be partisan in the matter of who should or should not occupy seats in this House.

I had not intended to speak on this point of order, Mr. Speaker, but there are one or two things which I think have not been made quite clear.	I am going to address my
remarks first to the very peculiar circumstances in which we find ourselves, and how these circumstances arose, with the idea of seeing that we quite appreciate the situation.
Let us clear away a little brushwood first.
I do not think there is very much doubt as to the crimes committed. It is quite true, as the Minister of Customs and Excise (Mr. Boivin) has pointed out, in making a strong argument in favour of Mr. Kennedy, that there is an appeal pending. But the minister did not go on to tell us that that appeal was taken on an absolute technicality; that no answer whatever is attempted to the charge that ballots had been switched, and 
that the facts are exactly as represented in the petition. I understand that there is no dispute as to that; so far I have heard of none in this debate. We can apparently take it for granted, therefore, that the facts are as represented, and that the crimes were committed as alleged in the petition.
Then let us move a little further. Is it a good thing that cognizance should be taken of these crimes; is it a good thing that the wrong should be righted? I suppose if we ask that question we put ourselves at once in the position of answering it; and the answer is in the affirmative. Here is an admitted case so far as the facts are concerned. I know nothing of what is going on or of what has gone on except what I have learned this afternoon. I asked my hon. friend the Minister of Customs on what date the petition which is making all the trouble here, this petition which is preventing Mr. Kennedy from doing the proper thing, this petition which is tying his hands and leaving him still with the stolen goods, was filed, and I have learned that it was filed on the 26th of February. I take it that my hon. friend's information is correct. I also learned that the petition was filed, not by Mr. Collins claiming his seat, not by any Conservative, not by anybody who was desirous of showing up these wrongs and having them remedied, but by the very party on whose behalf these crimes were committed. It is a petition launched in the Liberal interests. It is a petition brought by those who were the beneficiaries of the frauds committed and of the crimes that have been proven-the Liberal party. Why does the Liberal party take this stand?

May I interrupt my hon. friend? I do not think he wishes to misrepresent my attitude. I have already stated to the House that the only motive I have had in asking the Speaker's ruling on this matter is that not only as leader of the government, but as leader of the House, I have a certain obligation placed upon me in regard to matters that pertain to the orderly method of carrying on business in the House, and to see that the independence and freedom of members of parliament are protected and respected. I have felt that by asking Mr. Speaker to give his ruling on the point in question before we get into a general discussion, which it was the evident intention of the Controverted Elections Act to avoid, I was taking the course that would attain that end with the most dignity and decorum. That is the only reason I have had for bringing the matter up in this way.

My right hon.
friend is not following me. I am not referring to ihis point of order to-day at all. Mr. Speaker, I rise to a point of order. At six o'clock a point of
order was raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) with reference to some remark made in regard to the member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy) by the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton). I would ask the hon. member for West York to confine his remarks to the point of order, as I do not think the question of the personality of a member of the House of Commons should be considered in the discussion of a question such as the one now before the House.

I entirely agree with your ruling, Mr. Speaker, but so far I have not contravened it. I have made no reference whatever to the personal character of the hon. member. I am, however, referring to the exact situation which Your Honour in the first instance has to deal with, having regard to the point which you are asked to decide and what may happen as a result of the *ruling on that point of order. Parenthetically I would like to point out to my hon. friend who raised the point of order (Mr. Woodsworth) that I am rejoiced to see his change of heart. Earlier during this session precedent was something which was absolutely to be forgotten, not only by the hon. member himself but by the rest of the cohorts to your right, won-196J
Precedent, according to their argument, was something to be overlooked; parliament was all-strong and all-powerful and could do what it liked. Sometimes people change their minds and sometimes they do not.
I was pointing out, Mr. Speaker, that we have at the moment an admitted case of wrongdoing by an officer of this House. In the first instance, to make my point perfectly clear, I am not for one moment saying that, assuming Mr. Kennedy had been guilty of an offence under the Elections act, this House could, in view of the statute as to corrupt practices, take any action. I do not think the House could, and the only point here made -and it has not yet been answered-is that this House has the right to review the action of its officers. We have here an admitted case of a serious offence by an officer of this House. The hon. Minister of Customs and Excise reasons closely; I think he has probably stated the point more effectively for Mr. Kennedy than anybody else could. But with his closeness of reasoning he has admitted two things. He has admitted that this House has the right to review the action of its officers. In the next instance he has admitted it has the right to remedy the wrongs done by its officers. I need not go further than to take the two statements made by the hon. Minister of Customs and Excise. Let me repeat, so that there will be no doubt about it, that in the first instance this House has the right to review the action of its officers, and in the second instance this House has the right to remedy wrong arising from the improper conduct of its officers. The hon. member qualified those two statements 'by saying that their wrongs could not be righted; that the actions of the officer could not be considered until the proper time arrived; that they could not be considered now. Why? Simply because be have a petition pending. Is there any doilbt as to either of those statements or as to the ground upon which the hon. gentleman based his real argument?
Let me refer to one or two more of the hon. gentleman's arguments and I think, Sir, you will agree with me that the real gist of his contention was what I have just stated. He referred in the first instance to the mistake made by the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) when he referred to you, Sir, as my Lord, instead of Mr. Speaker. He seemed to regard that as a clear and unmistakable indication that in his heart of hearts the hon. member knew he was making his argument in the wrong place. I do not suppose I need stress the absurdity of that argument, but it seemed to be taken very

Peace River Election
seriously by hon. gentlemen across the way. I do not blame them for taking it seriously; in the absence of all real argument it would do; but I need not to say, Sir, that it is impossible that this petition should be thrown out because of a slip of the tongue.
His second point was that if this petition be received we shall have two trials proceeding at the same time. I think the hon. gentleman himself subsequently abandoned that point. We all know that the trial cannot go on, unfortunately-that is, unfortunately if the hands of this House be tied- while the House is in session. There is therefore nothing in that point.
His third point was that even if the petition were received Collins would not benefit by our receiving it because there would be obstruction in the committee and the like. I wonder whether it occurs to you, Sir, that a threat of improper action on the part of a committee is a reason for refusing the just rights of a petitioner. If it be not, there is nothing in the third point.
His fourth point was that if the House received the petition in this case, petitions to parliament would be in order every time a deputy returning officer was mistaken. This petitioner is not here on the ground of any mistake. My hon. friend stressed the question of mistakes; he sought to point out how mistakes could be easily made, honestly made. I wonder why? It is useless to talk about mistakes in the presence of absolute crime, admitted and proved. Why do I say "admitted"? I say admitted, because as I understand the matter-and I have made the same statement before without contradiction -the appeal relied upon by the Minister of Customs and Excise is taken merely upon a trifling technicality and not upon the merits of the case, not upon the facts that have been proved. Therefore I am well within the mark when I say that the real argument made by the Minister of Customs and Excise is that at the present time this House can do nothing. We must remember that that statement is made after his answer to my right hon. leader that parliament has the right to review the action of its officer and that parliament has the right to remedy wrongs committed by that officer.
I was referring to the question of the time not being ripe for dealing with this matter. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre pointed out that the hon. member whose seat is called in question could not take any part in these proceedings. I think he is enjoying them. He was enjoying them this afternoon; he was in the House at the time

the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre interfered in his behalf. He is present now. When I was interrupted I was pointing out what is the vital thing having regard to the one point really made by the Minister of Customs and Excise, namely, that the time is not ripe for action on the part of this House to rectify the wrong. Why not? We have this petition filed on the 26th day of February against the return of .the hon. gentleman. It was filed not by the petitioner or by a supporter of the petitioner, but by the petitioner's political opponent. The petitioner had nothing to do with it. It was filed on behalf of those who were interested in the crimes committed by Robb. We have this anomaly, that the reason why no action can be taken is because the real beneficiaries of Robb's crimes have lodged that petition! I wonder if it is possible for anyone to consider seriously the suggestion that nothing can be done now because the beneficiaries of this man's crimes have lodged a petition? If they are to be kept in charge of the proceedings in this way, it is a sorry day f)or justice.
I am aware of the provisions in the Elections Act as to other interests coming in and taking part in the proceedings. I am also aware how absolutely unworkable those things are. I have had to do with election petitions, and I know it is hard enough to fight election petitions when one has the right of way let alone having to carry on a three-cornered fight with a plaintiff in the position of sticking you in the back whenever he gets the chance.
How far have we got? We have reached the point that a political opponent has become useful to the government; that he has supported the government on every single vote prior to the 26th of February; that he was appointed on February 5 to the Customs inquiry committee on which this government s future depends; that he is being looked after by the government, while at the same time, on paper, supporters of this government are attacking the seat. Why? So that the hands of this House may be stayed, so that effect may be given to the argument made by the Minister of Customs and Excise. We have the right to correct wrongs committed by our servants; we have the right to discipline our officers. But, forsooth, we cannot do so as long as that petition stands. The government will hold the support of the hon. member for the session.
You, Mr. Speaker, are familiar with the election law, just as, I am sure, members of

I have not had occasion for some time now to consult the statute, but if, as I fancy, my recollection is correct, it used to be the law at one time at any rate, that any man could foe sworn and put into the box and compelled to say how he had voted. My impression is that this is still the law, and I have no doubt that the government is equally aware of the fact. But they know also that those people who were witnesses in the criminal trial could not be called and compelled to give evidence on an election petition.
Now, what is the situation to-day? Here we have an ostensibly proper Teturn, and if anything is wrong with it how shall we get around the difficulty? On a criminal trial electors can be called and sworn and compelled to give evidence, but this cannot be done in the case of an ordinary election petition. In view of that fact is there any reason why, in a matter in which right and justice are at stake, a petition of this kind should be refused? The argument that we are here attempting to set aside the Controverted Elections Act is without point; it falls entirely by the way No one is suggesting that anything is to be said against the hon. member, apart from the fact that knowing of this fraud, knowing that the seat was stolen from Collins by an officer of the House, he stands pat and exercises his functions as if he were indeed the representative of the electors of the constituency from which he comes, while as a matter of fact his election has been the result of the machinations of this officer. Apart from that knowledge on the hon. member's part, nothing can be said against him. So far as the petition itself is concerned there is nothing in its language in the slightest degree derogatory of the hon. gentleman.
What are the various circumstances that usually attend an action under the Controverted' Elections Act? They are acts on the part of the candidate, the acts of his agents, the purchase of votes, and allegations of that nature. Your Honour is familiar with them all. But not one of these circumstances enters into the question at present under review, the only point at issue being the conduct of an officer of thig House whom we seek to bring before parliament. I shall close by again pointing out what has been said by that hon. gentleman who, T think, has probably looked into the matter as closely as any one of us and who has spoken on behalf of the government. Certainly no hon. gentleman is more interested than he in seeing that in respect of himself he should present the strongest possible case. I refer to the Minister of Customs
(Mr. Boivin). What did he say? This House, he declared, has the right to inquire into the acts of its servants and to redress their wrongs; but it would appear the House cannot exercise that right so long as the other petition is there. Is parliament to be so gagged and stifled?

May an ordinary member venture to participate in a scientific debate? If I may 'be allowed a few minutes, Mr. Speaker, II should like to state with the utmost candour my humble opinion on this whole question. It seems to me that we must distinguish clearly between, on the one hand, the right of any Canadian citizen to petition parliament upon any question which he believes it is the duty of parliament to consider, and on the other hand the object of that petition. In my opinion the government would have done the right thing in receiving the petition which has now been presented to parliament, just as I think parliament should receive any other petition that might be submitted by a Canadian citizen in respect of any other question. Then, upon ascertaining the object of the petition, it would be for parliament, or some committee of parliament to consider whether the petition was one that might properly be dealt with by the House and adjudicated upon.
With due deference to the decision which you may give, Mr. Speaker, I do not think that until a petition is received by parliament it can be decided whether its object is such as to require consideration. I am not very much versed in the history of precedents and decisions in relation to cases of this kind, but as a Canadian citizen and a British subject I would seriously hesitate before denying to any Canadian the right to petition parliament touching any grievance which. he may think he has, and concerning which he seeks redress.
On the other hand, as regards the qualification of members of the House to sit in parliament, and respecting the circumstances connected with their election to the House of Commons, I think it was a wise decision which was arrived at some fifty years ago, to constitute a regular legal procedure through which anyone who desires to do so may contest the election of any member of parliament and ask that all the circumstances under which he was returned be probed. In this caSe, the simplest procedure would have been to receive the petition and submit it to the committee on Privileges and Elections, and on its being proven there that legal proceedings were being taken to find out whether the election of the member for Peace River is valid or
Peace River Election

Will the hon. member
permit a question?
Certainly.

If it is a fact that
witnesses at an election trial cannot be compelled to give evidence as to how they voted, then would it be possible to have the question raised in this petition adjudicated upon at an election trial?

I do not quite catch
the point made by the right hon. gentleman. As I understand it, parliament thought fit, a good many years ago,-and rightly so, I think-not to divest itself of the right to inquire into the doings of its officials with respect to elections, but to empower tribunals clothed with the necessary authority to look into such questions, to summon witnesses, to hear argument, and1 to decide whether or not wrongful acts have been committed by Subreturning officers or returning officers, or whether either of the candidates has been guilty of bribery or corruption or of any other wrongdoing which would justify those tribunals, acting in the name and under the authority of the parliament of Canada, to determine whether or not Mr. so-and-so is entitled to a seat in the House of Commons or should be excluded therefrom. Rightly or wrongly, parliament has decided, not to divest itself of its authority in these matters, but to delegate that authority to impartial tribunals, instead of leaving it to the will of a partisan majority in the House to decide whether or not a friend or an opponent of the dominant party should sit in the House. This I think, was a wise provision. If we deem it to be contrary to the privileges of parliament, let us repeal or amend that law, but as long as that statute stands as the expression of the will of parliament and the people let us respect it.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that it would be a most improper procedure on our part and not calculated to maintain in the minds of the people any respect for our parliamentary institutions, to say: Because we are in a hurry to take a seat from one party and give it to the other, we will take the case out of the hands of the tribunal which is now considering it and ourselves decide whether this man instead of the other man shall take his seat in this House, and so increase or diminish the majority of one party or the other.

Peace River Election
Therefore, so far as the merits of the question are concerned, I could not for one moment entertain the idea of having this petition considered on its merits, and say that the hon. member who was here a moment ago-and who I think should be out of this House while we are discussing his case -should have the question decided in his favour or against him. and that we should establish the right of his constituency to be represented in this House by Mr. Joe or Mr. John or Mt. Dick because of the action of one deputy returning officer out of two hundred, more or less.
On the other hand I do not think we should lay down the principle that any Canadian citizen should be denied access to this House with a petition for the redress of any grievance he may consider he has, whether he is right or wrong. I will admit there is not much logic in that statement, but if we examine the development of parliamentary government we must admit that there are many nonsenses connected with it which we must tolerate and accept as being among the guarantees of the liberty of the subject. Therefore, Sir, I am prepared to vote for the reception of this petition, just as I am prepared to vote for throwing it out of the purview of this parliament, because at present there is a judicial tribunal constituted under the laws of Canada to consider all the circumstances of the election.
Oh, oh.

Hon. gentlemen may
laugh, but I have seen many cases in which both parties were interested, in which the same spirit evinced to-day has shown itself in one way or another. Precedents are in vogue; principles are laid down, but it is certain that either through a judicial tribunal or through this House, any party looks after its own interests. It is just as well to admit that fact frankly as to conceal it hypocritically. But there are a few principles of law and government stronger and more enduring than the small and passing interests of any party or group of men. One of such, to which I have adhered all my life and to which I will always be true, is the principle that any citizen has a right to appeal to the parliament of Canada for the redress of any grievance. I will never go back on that. I have imbibed it in my study of parliamentary institutions, and no concern of friendship or of personal or collective advantage will make me depart from it.
On the other hand, considering the political conditions of our time and country, I think parliament was right in deciding that all
matters connected with electoral contests should be left to the decision of tribunals made up of supposedly impartial judges. When it comes to the merits of the question at issue, therefore, I consider that we have no moral right to decide upon the proper representative for this or any other constituency which may find itself in similar circumstances, because we have charged tribunals in every province of Canada to deal with these matters. These tribunals exercise the authority of parliament, under an act of parliament, which authority was, as a matter of fact, exercised by the old parliaments of Canada and England for many years. When it was found that such abuses of power, of partisanship and of passing majorities were occurring, parliament unanimously decided to leave to impartial tribunals the decision in matters of law as well as in matters of fact connected with the election of members of parliament. Upon these two principles I have acted, thought and fought during the twenty-five years I have been in the active public life of my country, and to them I remain true to-day.
To sum up these somewhat rambling remarks, I stand for the reception of this petition, because I would not deny to any fellow-citizen the right to petition this parliament. On the other hand, since the whole of this question has been debated in this House- quite improperly, I think-I stand for its reference to the proper tribunal instituted by this parliament to deal with all matters of this kind.

I
have listened most carefully to the speeches in connection with this most important subject, Mr. Speaker, and I must say that in my opinion the debate has shown that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) made a mistake in the way he brought this subject before the House.
He did not bring it before the House.
He brought in a motion this afternoon.

speechtext:
I made no
motion, but merely rose to a point of order to avoid discussion until the proper moment.

The Prime Minister made a mistake in raising this point of order at this time. My reason for that statement is that the speeches have nearly all been on the merits of the case, and it seems to me that the remarks of the Prime Minister should have been made before the committee,
Peace River Election

where they would have been heard and received with proper attention. I agree with the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) in regard to the reception of this petition; it seems to me this petitioner ought not to be refused access to parliament.
What is the point at issue? The point is whether Your Honour shall rule this petition may be received, or that the point of order raised by the Prime Minister is sound. Last fall writs were issued for an election; the chief electoral officer was instructed to carry out an election under the act, and the returning officer for Peace River was appointed. What was he told? He was instructed to return the writs to Ottawa on a certain date, and to state what candidate received the greatest number of votes. In this case the deputy returning officer made a false statement of the result of the voting at his poll. There is no dispute about that; he has been convicted of changing Iballots, and sentenced for the offence. Under these circumstances the writ was never returned to Ottaw'a in accordance with the act; in other words the writ did not properly state who had received the greatest number of votes. To say that this House has no authority over its own servants when misconduct of this kind has occurred is, it seems to me, going much further than anyone Should care to go.
Hon. gentlemen opposite have referred to a case back in 1874 and a later ease, but there *were two still later occasions on which matters of this kind came before the House. I do not know so much about the case in 1887, but I remember very well the Huron case, which came into this House, I think, in the year 1900. It was referred to a committee of the House, and was argued before that committee for weeks before a report was brought into the House. Therefore I claim that Your Honour has a specific precedent for allowing this petition to be received by the House and dealt with afterwards in such way as the House may see fit. In other words, I claim that the Huron precedent of 1900 is a perfect precedent from the point of view of Your Honour in deciding the question before us.
I was very much struck with one of the arguments put forward by my hon. friend from West York (Sir Henry Drayton), when he stated that under the Controverted Elections Act no power rested in the judge to compel any witness to say how he voted. In other words, the secrecy of the ballot has been guarded as strictly as it was possible to do it in our legislation, and as I understand it, no voter can be compelled in an election trial in the courts to say how he voted. That being

the case, I put it to my hon. friends opposite that there is no way in which a case of this kind can properly be tried under the Controverted Elections Act. If the voters cannot be compelled to say for whom they voted, how is it possible to bring home this scandal in connection with the action of the deputy returning officer in Peace River? What happened there was this. As I understand it, in general terms, the deputy returning officer having the ballot box in his charge and under his authority, opened or got someone else to open it, took out the ballots that were in it, and substituted for them a lot of other ballots marked in a different way. At the criminal trial of the deputy returning officer, certain electors appeared and volunteered the evidence that they had voted in a certain way. They satisfied the judge and jury that this officer had committed a very serious crime, and thereupon the judge sentenced him, and not only sentenced him but made the statement * that Collins was the man who should have been sitting as member. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I submit that on the merits of this case this petition ought to be received and referred to the committee on Privileges and Elections, where all these arguments as to why the case should be sent to the courts instead of being tried by a committee of this House could be submitted in a better way than they can possibly be argued here.
I am not a lawyer, and I am treading on dangerous ground when I deal with matters which lawyers have been discussing all afternoon. But if I am right in my understanding that under the Controverted Elections Act no voter can be forced to say how he voted, I would say that when parliament undertook to divest itself of jurisdiction in ordinary election trials for corruption and improper practices in an election as we understand them, it certainly did not undertake to divest itself of jurisdiction in a matter of this sort, where an officer of this House has committed the crime of changing the ballots and has wrongly declared the result of the poll, knowing that he was telling a falsehood. I do not believe the law passed in 1874 was intended to cover a case of that kind, particularly when this is the only place where a voter can be compelled to say how he voted. I submit to Your Honour, therefore, that as, at the election last fall, the returning officers were instructed to declare to this House the candidate receiving the greatest number of votes, and as this deputy returning officer in Peace River criminally changed the ballots and made a false return from bis own poll, knowing it

to be false, and as, in consequence, a false return of the result of the election in that constituency came into the office of the Chief Electoral Officer, Your Honour should declare that this is a petition which ought to be received by this House, and be dealt with by this House as it thinks proper.

It was that, since the passing of that act in England in 1888 and since the passing of a parallel act in Canada in 1873 these Houses-

That was the limit of its power; that was the contention of Sir John Thompson, and that con- * tention was quoted with approval by the right hon. leader of the government. Sir John Thompson quoted as authority for his position the opinions of Lord Seibome and Lord Coleridge expressed in 1870 in the British House of Commons, on which occasion those two eminent judicial authorities said:

But in all the cases in which petitions were considered. What would be the object of receiving the petition-unless an object which I do not for a moment suggest is what my hon. friends have in mind in opposing this point of order this afternoon-if after you have received it you cannot do anything with it? That is exactly the position my hon. friends would be in if a petition were received and this House has no jurisdiction over it. Why? Will any hon. member say that it would be a good thing for the conduct of elections, for parliamentary practice in Canada, to have the right of any member to sit in this House depend upon and be subject to a trial in which part of the tribunal would be an adverse majority in the House? I say that without meaning in the slightest degree to reflect upon the character of any member of any house of parliament.
That was the reason why parliament divested itself of jurisdiction. It was a good reason >n 1874; it is a good reason to-day, and in spite of all the solemn warnings that have been given this afternoon against making the great mistake of again refusing a petition, I ask in the name of everything that points to good parliamentary procedure: H hat would be the reason for receiving the petition if you could not act upon it and try it out after you had received it? I submit, with great respect to the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa), that it is useless to receive a petition if after you have it and look intc it you find no further facts than those which you already know, namely that it has been already submitted to a court of justice, and you can only return it and say you cannot act upon it. For that reason I represent most strongly that it would be establishing a most dangerous precedent and going baiek upon the rules of this House if we now departed from the established practice of over fifty years and received this petition. Far from impinging upon the rights of a Canadian petitioner by refusing to receive this petition. Your Honour would in my opinion be taking a dangerous step in admitting it. To receive the petition would be,
I respectfully submit, Sir, a procedure contrary to all the decisions which have been given by your illustrious predecessors through all these years.

In the course of his judgment Mr. Justice Strong said:
Another case is charge No. 6 in the notice of appeal, namely, the charge that the deputy returning officer at polling sub-division No. 2 in the township of Oneida, improperly marked ballots received by him at the said election, from electors before depositing the said ballots in the ballot-box, and thereby prevented the said ballots from being counted at the said election, and the ruling of the learned judge, rejecting the evidence on behalf of the petitioner which was tendered by h:m at the trial in support of the said charge.
Nothing could be made of this charge without admitting the evidence of voters to show how thfey voted. This I hold cannot be done. To do so would, in my opinion, be a direct violation of the act which requires secrecy.
Section 7, of the Dominion Elections Act, enacts:
This is the section I just read.
"No person who has voted at an election shall, in any legal proceeding questioning the election or return, be required to state for whom he voted."
It is no answer to this to say that secrecy is imposed for the benefit of the voter and that he can waive it, for I hold secrecy to be imposed as an absolute rule of public policy, and that it cannot be waived. The whole purview of the law is different from the English act and from the Ontario act. I am of opinion, therefore, that the learned judge rightly rejected the evidence though I may not be able to agree with the grounds he put it upon.
The Minister of Labour said that facts such as those appearing in this petition should undoubtedly be heard by some court, some judicial or supreme body; they should be ventilated, investigated and a decision rendered. Under this act there is only one body which can deal with such a question. The House of Commons of Canada has reserved to itself the right to determine such a matter It may seem strange that in the recent criminal trial, which took place in Alberta before Mr. Justice Walsh, evidence of voters stating for whom they voted was admitted. There is a very clear distinction between matters which come under the Controverted Elections Act, civil matters, and criminal matters. On that point I refer Your Honour to the case of Regina versus Saunders, 11 Manitoba reports, 1896, at page 563. Mr. Justice Dubuc held:
In the Haldimand election case, 15 S.C.R. 495, it was held that, under the provisions of section 71 of the act, secrecy of the ballot is an absolute rule of public policy, and it cannot be waived.
The court has to give effect to this statutory enactment; but the provision has a restrictive qualification which must not be overlooked. It says that no person shall be required to state for whom he voted in any legal proceeding questioning the election or return and not in any legal proceeding whatsoever. If this point had been raised in the trial of an election petition,-
And I ask you, Mr. Speaker, as well as my hon. friends opposite, to note particularly these words.

given in a trial on an indictment charging a criminal offence. When the witness Phillips was asked to state for which of the candidates he marked his ballot paper and voted, objection was raised to the question by the counsel for the defence on the ground that such evidence would be inconsistent with the secrecy of the ballot, and contrary to public policy. The learned Chief Justice, before whom the case was tried, allowed the question to be asked and answered, and it does not appear that the witness was unwilling to answer the question. There is nothing in the Dominion Elections Act, or in any other statute, declaring that, in the trial of a criminal offence, such a question cannot be asked and should not be answered.
I think, therefore, that the evidence was properly received, and that the first question submitted to the court should be answered in the affirmative.
Surely it is quite clear, Mr. Speaker, that there is no judicial body in existence in this country which can effectively inquire into the matters presented in this petition, nor is there any body other than parliament itself which can effectively give a remedy to the aggrieved party. That matter has clearly been placed beyond the jurisdiction of any court whatever, and there is only one body that can effectively deal with it.

Mr. Speaker, as the representative of
an important constituency in the great city of Winnipeg I deem it my duty to say something in this debate with regard to western conditions and western possibilities as well as conditions in general throughout Canada, in view of the fact that we are suffering in all parts of Canada to-day as a result of the lack of responsible government in our country. But what else have we a right to expect when we remember that no country in the civilized world has ever been known to approach anything like sound progressive administration under a compromise government? Who should know better than my right hon. friend opposite (Mr. Mackenzie King) that group government, compromise government, is nothing more than government from hand to mouth, nothing more than government that exists from day to day by way of "pull devil, pull baker?"
I would like to call my right hon. friend the Prime Minister as a living witness to the truth of this statement. During the recent campaign, from all the platforms of this country he made clear at all times that neither group government nor minority government was the kind of government wherewith to achieve great reforms. The Prime Minister went still further and said that neither group government nor minority government was the kind of government to meet Canada's needs to-day. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that every hon. member of this House agrees with that statement made by my right hon. friend upon these various occasions. We must agree because of the very conditions that exist to-day under the direction of my right hon. friend opposite. He must know-and that he does know, it is shown by his own statement-that it is im-

possible for him in the situation in which he finds himself to-day to do anything calculated to advance the best interests of this country. I appeal to my right hon. friend. Canada, the country in which he lives, has been very kind to him in the past, but now he sits in office here as the clog on the wheel. Why will he not do something in return that will be for the advantage of this country, which has done so much for him?
This is no time, Mr. Speaker, to toy, to barter,'to tinker as my right hon. friend is doing in respect of the government of this country. And what has been the effect upon the country? The effect has been to destroy confidence and security in this Dominion. All reasonable Canadians, in my humble judgment, should join in assisting to create that sound public opinion by which alone stability of government can be restored. Party government in the past may have had its difficulties, but we must never overlook the fact that party government has made this Dominion of Canada what it is to-day. In my judgment it is only under that form of government that confidence and security can be restored in this country. Under the administration of my right hon. friend loss of confidence and security has done more than anything else during the past eight or ten years to retard the progress of our Dominion. In proof of that 10 p.m. statement I am going, to give you just a few brief figures which, to my mind, make it abundantly clear that our country is going back, and going back rapidly, under the administration of my right hon. friend. These figures furnish, in my judgment, a very clear index as to conditions in all parts of Canada. I am going to show how much was collected in income tax when my right hon. friend came into power, and then compare that with the amount that is being collected to-day.
In 1921-22, the year my right hon. friend came into power, 18,840 farmers paid in income tax $1,299,104.54. In 1924-1925 only 3,061 farmers in Canada were able to pay income tax to the amount of $162,944.74; in other words, 15,780 farmers who were able to pay income tax when my right hon. friend came into power are not able to pay a dollar of income tax to-day.

I have given you the

Conditions in the western provinces, I may say, have been very much disturbed as the result of the actions of the Progressive party during these two elections, and, I deem it my duty to let this House and the country know the manner in which they have been carrying on their elections in the past.
Now they talk about the tariff and about the seriousness of the taxation placed upon the farmers of western Canada. I want to say to them: Give the farmers in Manitoba and in western Canada generally a market for that which they produce, and they will neither ask for nor accept remedies born of politea! fright such as we had introduced the other day by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister. The progress of the farmers of western Canada has been retarded by my friend from Brandon and by my friend the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) in the matter of their getting what is coming to them in transportation costs. This is a serious matter to the farmers of the west, and it is an equally serious matter to the people of the east, because I want them to understand that they are just as much interested in the condition of western Canada as are those who live there. The people of eastern Canada must never overlook the fact that railways and their workers, manufacturers and their employees, banks and their staffs can only preserve their positions and their property so long as the farmers of western Canada are assured of a fair living wage for that which they produce. The greatest enemies that the farmers of the west have had to contend against in securing that fair living wage are my hon. friend from Brandon and my hon. friend from Regina. They are two of the greatest sinners in this House in retarding the progress of the farmers of western Canada.
Now, in 1900 the government of Manitoba of which I was a member felt that it owed a
